profile.name: Mikaël Lenaertz
profile.title: Senior Software Engineer
profile.summary: Senior software engineer with 12+ years experience designing and operating distributed systems at scale, from mission-critical dispatch platforms to AWS Lambda's control plane. I enjoy ambiguous, high-stakes problems and owning solutions from root cause to production.

intro: My fascination with software didn't start in a classroom; it began the moment my family got access to the internet. Wondering how programs worked under the hood, I wrote my first lines of C at fifteen. That first "Hello, World!" on the terminal sparked a lifelong drive for low-level performance and algorithmic efficiency.

At university, while earning my Master's in Computer Science with Great Distinction and a Master's in Computer Engineering, I thrived on hands-on implementation projects: multiplayer game tournament engines built over raw sockets, swarm intelligence algorithms like Ant Colony Optimization applied to shortest-path problems, and a soccer simulation where I replaced the default behaviours with machine learning decision models. That early passion for algorithms led me to competitive programming, where I learned to dissect complex performance bottlenecks under real time pressure. What stuck with me from those years wasn't the algorithms themselves, it was the habit of treating every inefficiency as a problem worth understanding all the way down. That habit has shaped how I've approached every system I've touched since.

paragraphs: After graduating, I was looking for a first opportunity with real impact, and Intergraph's public safety systems offered exactly that. I started my professional career building emergency call-taking and dispatching platforms for the Belgian Police and Fire-Medical departments, working across C++, C# and Oracle DB in an environment where reliability and performance were core requirements.

A new requirement came in that needed a business analyst, so I stepped up to fill that gap myself. I built out the proof of concept, and based on that work I was asked to lead and onboard a team of three external developers to help bring the product to life, taking on the Tech Lead role for the combined effort while continuing to code alongside them.

One of the satellite applications had tightly coupled modules that made independent development difficult, so I designed a dynamic C# plugin framework using reflection to replace the fat-client codebase, cutting time-to-market significantly. I also solved a persistent database update bottleneck: refactoring the legacy Soundex phonetic algorithm with a trie data structure, reverse-engineering the un-indexed queries underneath it, and batching the updates brought an eight-hour process down to a few minutes. Alongside that, I helped the team build our Jenkins CI/CD pipeline from scratch, which ended the manual deployment errors we'd been living with.

I joined SWIFT wanting to deepen my C++ expertise, aiming to eventually work on problems closer to the machine. My early years there were spent maintaining a cross-platform C++98 messaging engine running across Linux, Windows, AIX and SunOS: refactoring 1000-line legacy functions into something maintainable, consolidating a scattering of database tools into a single migration framework, and building custom thread-safe components to keep the system stable under high throughput.

My role expanded when my team, seeing that the cloud engineering group was short on resources, put me forward as a candidate to help transition our core messaging platform into an event-driven microservices architecture using Java, Apache Kafka, JPA and Docker. That move ended up shifting me away from the C++ specialization path I'd originally set out on, toward broader distributed systems work instead. I found myself working closely with product and UX to make sure the new architecture actually matched how the system was used, while building out automated testing to keep pace with the changes.

Driven by curiosity, in my second year I spent one day a week in SWIFT's R&D Lab engineering an NLP pipeline, using spaCy, CNNs and Bloom embeddings, to parse unstructured text into structured physical address data. That work matured enough to eventually be taken over by a dedicated product team.

After several years there, I took a break and left for Australia, spending three months visiting friends there and a month in Vietnam. The four months after I got back were spent job hunting, difficult going given COVID and how uncertain the market was at the time, until my previous Tech Lead vouched for me to rejoin SWIFT, this time on the instant payments connectivity team.

There, I worked on a Dockerized application built from multiple microservices in Java, using gRPC and queue adapters to connect them. My biggest impact came after our testers moved on to other roles: I automated deployment, integration testing, and performance testing to cover the gap they'd left behind, building a full end-to-end load-testing stack with Ansible to catch bottlenecks before they reached production.

Technology being the business itself was what pulled me toward AWS. I joined to work on the Lambda control plane, the low-level infrastructure responsible for orchestrating, storing, optimising and deploying serverless functions globally. There, I took a leading technical role in delivering my team's contribution to major initiatives, including Lambda Managed Instances, a runtime flexibility initiative, and an overhaul of the code deletion workflow.

One of the pieces I'm proudest of was rewriting the pipeline that packages and optimises Lambda functions, moving it from Java to a concurrent, channel-based design in Go that roughly halved processing latency.

Separately, another system hit real trouble when a legacy background job model started failing to scale in one of our largest regions, putting global rollouts at risk. I designed and shipped a deduplicated database model within a week to resolve it.

Not every problem I dealt with was a design choice, some just had to be found. After the service migrated from the US to Ireland, the team started getting paged constantly, sometimes over fifty times a week, dozens of those in the middle of the night, because of API load shedding despite our instances being heavily over-provisioned. Tracing it back took a while: high-volume workloads had quietly broken a background job architecture that was scanning the entire database daily. Fixing the query pattern and adding sharding ended the pages entirely. That stretch also taught me something about myself: running on too little sleep while trying to fight every fire at once just isn't sustainable, and I've since gotten better at recognising when I'm stretched too thin and need to step back or bring someone else in, rather than pushing through solo.

Beyond the code itself, I also took on reworking how the team ran day to day. Our Scrum process was clunky for a team shipping several times a day, standups dragged with little engagement, and planning didn't match how we actually worked. I restructured the rituals around the way the team actually shipped, and watched something I hadn't expected: once the formal meetings got lighter, people started resolving things with each other directly instead of saving every question for the next standup.

closing: After a bit over three years in Dublin, my wife and I decided to move back to Belgium, wanting to settle before our child got older rather than uproot them further down the line. I'm back in Brussels now, looking for what comes next.

roles.summary: Worked on AWS Lambda's control plane, responsible for orchestrating, storing, and optimizing the creation and updates of serverless functions at scale, allowing customers to run them without having to provision or manage servers. Drove cross-team technical initiatives, operational excellence, and engineering mentorship throughout the role.
highlights: Led the technical delivery of my team's contribution to three major Lambda control plane initiatives, including Lambda Managed Instances, a runtime flexibility initiative, and a code deletion workflow overhaul, owning each end to end from design through deployment and operational readiness.
Designed and implemented a channel-based pipeline architecture in Go enabling flexible parallel processing of function optimizations, reducing end-to-end processing time by 50%

Resolved recurring background job failures affecting thousands of functions, work that also deduplicated code artifacts, cutting artifact storage nearly 50%, and drove a broader S3 storage reduction of 70% (200PB).

Rewrote the team's integration testing frameworks to enable independent execution, broaden business-critical coverage and eliminate security liabilities, reducing weekly rollbacks from 20+ to near-zero.
Built multiple AI agents and skills for automated report generation and operational investigation, built on Kiro, AWS's AI-powered development environment.
Resolved a day-one bug in function optimisations that had silently caused random failures for every ~10,000 function creations or updates since the service launched.

experience.company: SWIFT – Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication

roles.summary: Joined the team building the instant payments connectivity solution on the Swift Network, receiving messages from financial institutions via REST APIs and message queue brokers and forwarding them securely to the network. Designed and delivered features that improved the reliability and scalability of the solution.
highlights: Rebuilt end-to-end test automation after the team lost both QA engineers, consolidating scattered Robot Framework suites into one repository and generalising tests across IBM MQ, ActiveMQ and REST endpoints, with Ansible-provisioned multi-node environments for automated compatibility testing.
Modernised Jenkins and CloudBees pipelines, migrating from imperative scripts to declarative pipelines with shared libraries to modularise logic across components.

Automated performance testing by parameterising JMeter scripts and integrating load tests into the Jenkins pipeline, streaming live metrics into InfluxDB with Grafana dashboards for real-time regression visibility.

roles.summary: Part of the back-end team building the cross-platform messaging interface for secure financial information exchange between banking organisations and corporate customers, deployable on Windows, Red Hat, SunOS and AIX.
highlights: Developed a cloud-based microservice to manage relationships between financial institutions, enabling secure and reliable financial information exchange.
Built a Named-Entity Recognition (NER) system as part of an NLP proof-of-concept, extracting structured address data from unstructured, free-field text.

Replaced Oracle-specific backup and restore tooling with a unified, application-driven migration framework, refactoring complex legacy C++98 functions to decouple database logic without disrupting backup operations on a mission-critical financial messaging system.

roles.summary: Analysed, designed, implemented and supported mission-critical software for public safety, working on call-taking and dispatching solutions for the Belgian Federal and Local Police and the Fire-Medical Departments.
highlights: Stepped up to fill a business analyst role on a new requirement, delivering the proof of concept and subsequently leading and onboarding a team of three external developers, while continuing to code alongside them.

Designed and implemented a dynamic C# plugin framework using reflection to replace a satellite application's tightly coupled fat-client codebase, enabling independent feature development and significantly cutting time-to-market.
Optimised the Soundex algorithm with a trie and batched database updates, cutting update times from 8 hours to minutes.
Built internal tooling (XML comparator, file format validator) and automated build patching and installation, significantly reducing manual work across the team.
